title: Two Indian Nationals Plead Guilty in PayPal Refund Scam Targeting Elderly Arkansas Resident
excerpt: Gajera Prashant and Dharaben Bavadiya were arrested in a Gentry police sting operation after attempting to collect cash from an elderly victim who had been duped through a fake PayPal refund scheme.
body:
• Gajera Prashant and Dharaben Bavadiya, both Indian nationals, have pleaded guilty to theft charges in Gentry, Arkansas, after being caught in a police sting operation tied to a PayPal refund scam.
  • The pair were arrested on April 21 while attempting to collect money from an elderly victim who had been tricked through a fake PayPal refund notification.
  • The case is part of a broader pattern of India-linked tech support and refund fraud rings that the FBI estimates cost elderly Americans more than $3.4 billion in 2023 alone.

Sting Operation in Small-Town Arkansas

Gentry Police in northwest Arkansas arrested Gajera Prashant and Dharaben Bavadiya on April 21 on theft charges after a sting operation involving a PayPal refund scam targeting an elderly resident. Both have since pleaded guilty, according to local law enforcement reports confirmed in an August 20 report.

https://x.com/bluelivesmtr/status/2090906793836699863

The scheme followed a pattern that federal agencies have documented extensively in recent years: scammers contact victims — often elderly — claiming that PayPal or another financial services company owes them a refund. The victim is guided through steps that appear to show a large overpayment deposited into their bank account. Scammers then demand the victim return the supposed excess, typically through cash, cryptocurrency, or gold.

In the Gentry case, police set up a controlled operation after the elderly victim reported the scam. Prashant and Bavadiya arrived to collect money from the victim and were arrested at the scene.

A Growing Pattern of India-Linked Refund Fraud

The Gentry arrests are the latest in a steady stream of federal and state cases involving Indian nationals operating as couriers, or "runners," in fraud networks that originate from call centres in India. The schemes typically involve call centre operators who initiate the fraud remotely, while couriers based in the United States collect cash, gold, or other valuables from victims in person.

In a separate but similar case this year, a federal jury in Florida convicted Atharva Shailesh Sathawane, a 22-year-old Indian national, of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering after he was caught in a sting operation linked to a PayPal refund scam. Court documents showed Sathawane was involved in more than 30 transactions across multiple states, contributing to nearly $8 million stolen from elderly victims. He faces up to 20 years on each count.

In Ohio, federal authorities arrested Indian nationals Tejas Patel and Navya Bhatt on money laundering charges tied to a network that included PayPal fraud, fake Microsoft computer repair schemes, and cryptocurrency-related scams. Victims in Ohio, Michigan, and Pennsylvania lost tens of thousands of dollars each, with one Toledo woman handing over more than $40,000 in cash after suspects falsely claimed to represent the Federal Trade Commission.

"If you pause these scams for just 10 seconds, many of them will just fall apart."

— Detective Justin Torres, Gainesville Police Department, Florida

How the PayPal Refund Scam Works

Federal investigators have outlined a consistent playbook. Victims receive an email or pop-up claiming they owe money or are due a refund from PayPal, Microsoft, or another recognisable company. When they call the number provided, a scammer walks them through steps that include granting remote access to their computer.

The scammer then manipulates what the victim sees on screen — making it appear that a large sum has been accidentally deposited into their bank account. Victims are told the only way to return the "overpayment" without tax penalties is to withdraw cash, buy gold, or use a cryptocurrency ATM.

In many cases, couriers travel to the victim's home to collect the cash or gold in person. One Florida victim, an 85-year-old retiree, lost $200,000 after buying gold coins and handing them to a courier who arrived at his door with a pre-arranged password. Another victim in that case lost $4.9 million.

Scale of the Problem

The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center reported that Americans over 60 lost more than $3.4 billion to fraud in 2023, with tech support and refund scams among the top categories. India-based call centres have been identified as a primary source of these operations, with the FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, and India's Enforcement Directorate cooperating on cross-border investigations.

Federal sentencing in related cases has been severe. A courier ringleader in a separate India-linked scheme received a 15-year-and-eight-month prison sentence and was ordered to pay more than $3.5 million in restitution. Multiple co-conspirators in that case received sentences ranging from 18 months to five years.

For diaspora communities, the cases carry a dual concern: the pattern of Indian nationals being recruited as money mules — often on student or overstayed visas — and the reputational damage to the broader community from high-profile fraud prosecutions.
